signals.source_text: Lt. Gen. Joseph Jarrard, deputy commander of NORTHCOM, said this month: "We don't have the sensors... We are ill-equipped right now to handle something like that... We're seeing it used on a daily basis around the world, and we've got to figure out how to mitigate that threat. But we're not there yet." He also separately said: "Detection is obviously the biggest issue, and so how we are able to detect is one of our biggest concerns right now." Meanwhile, the counter-drone vendor pitch for 2026 is almost uniformly "layered defense" — stack an RF detector, an AI-video classifier, a kinetic or non-kinetic effector, and call it depth. Several recent product launches lead with AI video fused to RF as the differentiator. Here's the disconnect. A three-star just told the public the bottleneck is sensors and detection, not effector diversity. And detection at swarm tempo isn't really a sensor-count problem — it's a track-correlation problem. Every additional modality is another stream that has to be time-aligned, classified, and reconciled with the others before anyone can act. Add a sensor without solving fusion latency and false-positive suppression, and you've made the decision harder, not easier, against a swarm that's inside your OODA loop in single-digit seconds. If you're building in this space, the question worth obsessing over isn't "what's my next sensor modality." It's "how fast and how reliably does my fusion engine resolve conflicting tracks into one actionable picture" — because that's the gap NORTHCOM's own leadership is naming publicly, not a gap in sensor variety. Where do you think the real bottleneck is — sensor coverage, fusion latency, or engagement authority? #DoW #Defense #Autonomy #CUAS

signals.source_text: Why did Network School choose Kazakhstan over 10+ countries? A new conversation with Balaji Srinivasan has just premiered across Trusted Kazakhstan, Astana Hub, and Network State Podcast. Network School is building a global community for people who want to learn tech, work remotely, build companies, and live alongside other ambitious people. Kazakhstan is set to become one of the first major global hubs for this model. In the conversation, Balaji Srinivasan, founder of Network School and former CTO of Coinbase, joins Rinata Ilyubayeva , Managing Director at Astana Hub, and host Thorsten Gutmann to discuss why Kazakhstan stood out among more than 10 countries considered for Network School’s expansion. The discussion goes beyond the decision itself. It explores: • why Astana can become a destination for global tech talent • how digital nomads can contribute to Kazakhstan’s innovation ecosystem • new approaches to education and lifelong learning • how global and local talent can build companies together • Kazakhstan’s growing focus on AI, emerging technologies, and new industries • what the cities and communities of the future could look like One of the central ideas of the conversation is simple: Kazakhstan has the opportunity not only to attract global talent, but to create an environment where people can build, scale, and take tech to international markets. For us at Astana Hub, this is also part of a broader ambition: to make Kazakhstan a place where international founders, engineers, creators, and investors can connect with local talent and build globally competitive tech businesses.
